sam.voice: Calm, crisp incident commander. Asks for impact, hypothesis, next step and ETA. Keeps a running timeline and repeats decisions back.
sam.agenda: Run the incident: get a hypothesis, a mitigation, and regular updates. Starts by blaming the search index and wants a full reindex and a status message about delayed results. If the candidate shows evidence that it is ours in the browser (every response matches its own query on all replicas; the RUM log shows render for results_for='sh' after the one for 'shoes' in the same session with stale=true; the API answered 'sho' and 'sh' slowly (650 to 1,150 ms) and 'shoes' fast (94 ms); stale renders are 94% in sessions where a short prefix answered after a longer one; 2026.46.2 tabs that search from 3 characters show 0.1%; the metric stayed flat after the reindex), he corrects the status message, stops the reindex if asked, and asks what to do instead. He can flip remote-config flags if the candidate proposes it (the app polls remote config every 5 minutes): search_min_chars from 1 to 3 (short prefixes are the slow ones, so stale renders drop sharply; shoppers lose results for 1-2 characters), and typeahead off (search only on Enter: removes the race but conversion on search drops, he would need Mara's OK). He asks about a hotfix: what is the risk, how long until the fix reaches shoppers (a web release; people keep tabs open for hours on old bundles, so how do old tabs get it), and how will they know it worked (search_stale_render_rate). Asks whether shoppers need anything (status page update, support macro) and why the metric did not page anyone (no alert, KES-277). Will only agree to call it resolved once there is a mitigation in place or a fix ready and a plan for the status page and the alert; then asks for a one-paragraph summary.
sam.knows: Metric values, support volume, the remote-config flags in the storefront notes, and that the reindex is running if he started it. Does NOT read code and does not know the root cause.

flaws.title: Says to revert a failed update to the previous value
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks what quantity to show when an update request fails, or how to roll back an optimistic update.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say keep the quantity from before the click and put it back on failure: that is the standard optimistic-update rollback and it is simple, nothing more is needed.
flaws.correctBehavior: With several quick changes the 'previous' value is itself an optimistic value the server never confirmed. A failure must go back to the last quantity the server confirmed (the ticket says so), and newer wanted quantities are dropped.

flaws.title: Says titles are plain catalog text so templates or raw() are fine
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks how to render the line title or button labels in the cart, or whether they need to escape them.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say titles are plain text from our catalog, so building the markup with a template string or using raw() is fine and escaping is over-engineering; h() is for the static parts.
flaws.correctBehavior: Titles are written by independent sellers and the ticket says they must be escaped (a title with <, & or a quote breaks the markup and is an XSS risk). Let h()/renderToString escape them; raw() is only for static markup.

flaws.title: Says to keep showing the quantity the shopper asked for when stock is short
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks Mara what the cart should show when the server confirms fewer items than the shopper asked for.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say keep showing what they asked for so it does not feel like an error, we can sort the stock out at checkout.
flaws.correctBehavior: Her own ticket says the line shows the server's quantity with an 'Only n of <title> available' announcement. Showing an amount that cannot be bought makes the subtotal wrong and the shopper finds out at payment.

flaws.title: Says seller titles are moderated and HTML is stripped, so raw() is safe
flaws.trigger: The candidate raises that the highlighted title is rendered with raw() or that a seller title could contain markup.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say titles are moderated and HTML is stripped when a listing is created, so they are safe and escaping again is redundant.
flaws.correctBehavior: Moderation is not an escaping layer: sellers can edit titles after review, imports and other services write titles, and a filter that strips tags can be bypassed. Escape at output, every time, and keep raw() for markup we wrote.

issues.title: The query is put into a regular expression as is
issues.detail: The query is whatever the shopper typed. 'c++', '(', '[' or '?' make new RegExp throw a SyntaxError inside renderSearch, which happens on a render after the request has already succeeded: the results area throws and the page can go blank for a very ordinary search (c++ books, '(' typos). Other patterns can backtrack badly. Escape the query or use string search instead of a regex.

issues.title: Seller titles are rendered unescaped with raw()
issues.detail: raw() skips escaping, so a seller title like runs in every shopper's browser who searches for it (stored XSS, with access to the session and the checkout). 'Moderated' is not an escaping layer. Escape the title, then add only the tags we generate.

issues.title: It highlights against what is in the box, not what the results are for
issues.detail: While typing, the box says 'shoes' but the results on screen can still be for 'sh' (this is exactly the INC-0912 window), so the highlight is wrong or missing. Use resultsFor, the query the results answer.

issues.title: The test only covers a plain word
issues.detail: One test with 'shoes' and a title that is plain text would not have caught the regex crash, the escaping problem, or the stale query. Ask for tests with special characters (c++, (, &, <), a case difference, no match, and an empty query.

issues.title: It escapes the title first and then searches the escaped text
issues.detail: v2 fixes the XSS but now searches inside the escaped string. A query of 'amp', 'lt', 'gt', 'quot' or '&' matches the entity text itself: 'Tom & Jerry' becomes 'Tom & Jerry' and a search for 'amp' wraps the middle of the entity, producing broken markup ('&<mark>amp</mark>;' shows a literal '&'), and the test only covers c++. Find the matches in the raw title, then escape each piece (the matched and the unmatched parts) separately before joining them with <mark>.

incident.rootCause: search.setQuery fires a request on every keystroke and whichever answer arrives last wins: nothing ties an answer to the latest input. Since 2026.47 (Nov 24) the box searches from the first character, and since last night's index rebuild (v412) 1-2 character prefix queries are slow (p95 about 1.5 s against 180 ms for 3+ characters) because they fan out to every shard. So when someone types 'shoes' quickly, the answers for 'sho' and 'sh' (slow) arrive after the answer for 'shoes' (fast) and replace it: the box says 'shoes' and the page shows results for 'sh'. It is not the index (all replicas are on v412 and every response matches its own query), not the browser (same rate on Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge), and it is not new code: the race existed before, but the 3-character minimum and a fast backend hid it (stale rate 0.2%, with 2026.46.2 tabs that still search from 3 characters at 0.1%). The fix is to give each request a sequence number (or abort the previous request) and ignore any answer or error that is not for the latest input; clearing the box must also invalidate requests in flight. A debounce reduces the requests but does not remove the race.
keyPoints: Uses evidence from the logs (render for results_for='sh' after 'shoes' with stale=true in the same session; 'sh' answered in 1,150 ms and 'shoes' in 94 ms; the same stale rate on all browsers; 0.1% on 2026.46.2 tabs that search from 3 characters; 94% of stale renders have a shorter prefix arriving late; index health 6/6 at v412 and zero mismatches; the stale rate unchanged after the reindex).
Pushes back on blaming the index and on the status message and the reindex, with evidence.

Proposes a fast mitigation separately from the code fix (search_min_chars from 1 to 3, or typeahead off) and names the tradeoffs (no results for 1-2 characters, search conversion if typeahead goes off).

Fixes the race: a sequence number or an AbortController so only the latest request may change the state, covering errors too, and clearing the box; may add a debounce but does not rely on it. Thinks about how the fix reaches shoppers who keep tabs open on old bundles (version skew, a refresh banner, remote config).
Writes a regression test that fails on the old code (answers out of order, late failure, clearing in flight).
Posts regular, structured status updates (impact, cause, next step, ETA) and corrects the status page.

Thinks about remediation: an alert on search_stale_render_rate (KES-277), a contract test with out-of-order answers, a support macro, why the 3-character minimum was lowered without a guard, a postmortem.
Does not just say yes: names the risks (Wednesday 6 PM freeze, a change right after an incident, other teams' approval).

Raises that a third-party script on the cart and checkout pages is a security and PCI-scope problem (it can read card fields and the session), needs a content security policy and security approval, can hurt performance (blocking script, layout shift) and needs consent handling; offers safe alternatives (cart page only, loaded async after consent, behind a flag, server-side integration or a tag manager review, not on payment fields).

Raises that the 'cart reserved for 10:00' countdown is only honest if the backend actually reserves stock (today it does not); it must use the server's expiry time, not the browser's clock (clocks are wrong and tabs sleep); says what happens at 0:00; accessibility (no per-second announcements, respect reduced motion).
Asks the clarifying questions that matter (who approves scripts on payment pages? does inventory support reservations? does legal care about false urgency?).
Offers options: ship KES-318 and highlighting for Thursday, the script on the cart page only after security review, the countdown once reservations exist (or a truthful 'low stock' message now).
Gives an estimate or confidence level, and leaves the decision to Mara with the tradeoffs clear. Answers on the ticket as asked.

Challenges 'prices rarely change and the refresh fixes it': showing yesterday's price or stock next to a checkout that charges today's erodes trust; cached data should not contain prices, or the cache must be revalidated before it is shown as current.
Stale-while-revalidate is the same race as today's incident: the fresh answer must be tied to the latest input and must not replace newer results; needs request sequencing.

The key is only the query: results depend on locale, currency, market, logged-in segment and the index version, so the key must include them (or a cache version) and entries must be dropped on a release or index change.
Privacy: search history is personal data and is readable by anyone on a shared computer; don't store it by default, offer clearing on logout.

localStorage is synchronous, small (about 5 MB) and can throw (quota, private mode, disabled): entries need a size cap and eviction (LRU), a version, try/catch around every access, and a fallback; cap what is stored (ids and titles, not the whole response).
Rollout to 100% in one release with no flag or metric: use a flag, a percentage rollout, and measure (stale render rate, conversion, errors).
Tone: specific, constructive, ties it to the incident.
States what is done (incident mitigation and fix status, KES-318 progress) and what is open (PR #412 changes requested, Mara's script and countdown answer, RFC comment).

Lists incident follow-ups: the status page correction, stopping or finishing the reindex, reverting search_min_chars or typeahead after the fix ships, an alert for search_stale_render_rate, a contract test, the postmortem.
Short and scannable, with owners or next steps.
